chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Muhammad al-Wabishi, who said:

I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Be cautious of your personal desires just as you are being cautious of your enemies, for there is nothing more inimical to the men than their following of their own personal desires and the harvest of their tongues'.

key_terms.أَهْوَاءٌ: Personal desires or whims; plural of هوا

ai.seo_question: What are the two main internal enemies a Muslim must guard against according to this hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elevates the internal struggle against nafs (self) to the level of jihad against external foes, highlighting that unbridled desires are more insidious than visible enemies. The metaphor of 'harvests of tongues' underscores how unchecked whims manifest in speech, leading to doctrinal deviation and social discord, a key concern in Shia epistemology. This teaching aligns with the concept of 'tazkiyah' (purification of the soul), where controlling one's inner impulses is prerequisite to spiritual integrity.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Muhammad Al Wabishi who said,

‘I heard Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> saying: ‘Be cautious of your personal desires just as you are being cautious of your enemies, for there is nothing more inimical to the men than their following of their own personal desires and the harvest of their tongues’.
en.sarwar: 1. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from ibn Mahbub from abu Muhammad al-Wabishi who has said the following: “
I heard abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) saying, ‘Be afraid of your desires just as you fear your enemies. Nothing is a more dangerous enemy to men than following their desires and what their tongues harvest.’”
